docs.title: Robot Architecture
docs.text:
In previous lectures, we discussed how robots think and make decisions.

Now we move to a more fundamental question:

How is a robot physically built?

A robot is not just software. It is a system composed of interconnected subsystems.

Understanding this architecture helps us design, analyze, and debug robots properly.

docs.title: Robot Architecture Overview
docs.text:
A robot can be divided into three major subsystems:

  1. Motion System
  2. Recognition System
  3. Control System

These subsystems work together in a closed loop.

Recognition → Control → Motion

docs.title: Motion System
docs.text:
The motion system is responsible for physical movement.

It includes:

  • Manipulator (links and joints)
  • End-effector
  • Actuators
  • Transmission mechanisms (belt, gear, linkage)

This subsystem answers:

How does the robot move?

docs.title: Example: Industrial Robotic Arm
docs.text:
Consider a robotic arm in a car manufacturing plant.

  • The arm rotates at joints.
  • Motors drive the links.
  • Gears transmit torque.
  • A gripper holds metal parts.

This entire structure is the motion subsystem.

docs.title: Why This Example Fits
docs.text:
The robotic arm:

  • Has joints (manipulator structure)
  • Uses motors (actuators)
  • Uses gears (transmission)
  • Produces physical motion

It directly demonstrates how the motion system converts energy into mechanical movement.

docs.title: Recognition System
docs.text:
The recognition system allows the robot to sense its environment.

It includes:

  • Sensors
  • Signal conversion (ADC)
  • Basic processing

This subsystem answers:

What is happening around me?

docs.title: Example: Warehouse Robot
docs.text:
A warehouse robot uses:

  • Camera to detect shelves
  • LiDAR to measure distance
  • Encoders to measure wheel rotation

These sensors allow it to understand position and obstacles.

docs.title: Why This Example Fits
docs.text:
Without sensors:

  • The robot cannot detect shelves.
  • It cannot avoid obstacles.
  • It cannot localize itself.

Recognition is the foundation of intelligent behavior.

docs.title: Control System
docs.text:
The control system makes decisions and generates commands.

It includes:

  • Digital controller
  • Algorithms
  • DAC
  • Amplifiers

This subsystem answers:

What should I do next?

docs.title: Example: Line-Following Robot
docs.text:
A line-following robot:

  • Reads sensor values.
  • Controller computes error.
  • PID algorithm calculates correction.
  • Motor speed is adjusted.

docs.title: Why This Example Fits
docs.text:
The controller:

  • Processes sensor data.
  • Makes decision.
  • Sends motor command.

This demonstrates how control connects sensing and motion.

docs.title: System-Level Understanding
docs.text:
A robot is not a single machine.

It is an integration of:

  • Sensing (Recognition)
  • Thinking (Control)
  • Acting (Motion)

If any subsystem fails:

  • No sensing → blind robot
  • No control → unstable robot
  • No motion → useless robot

Good robotics engineering means designing these subsystems to work reliably together.

docs.title: Part 2 — Motion System
docs.text:
In the architecture overview, we said:

Motion system = how the robot physically moves.

Now we break it down clearly.

docs.title: 1. What Is the Motion System?
docs.text:
The motion system converts energy into controlled movement.

It includes:

  • Manipulator (structure)
  • End-effector (interaction tool)
  • Actuator (energy source)
  • Transmission (power transfer)

Think of it like this:

Energy → Actuator → Transmission → Link → End-effector → Motion

docs.title: 2. Manipulator (Robot Structure)
docs.text:
A simple 2-link arm:

Link0--Joint1--Link1--Joint2--Link2

Explain:

  • Links = rigid bodies
  • Joints = allow motion
  • Base = fixed reference

The manipulator is the mechanical skeleton of the robot.

A manipulator consists of:

  • Links
  • Joints (Revolute or Prismatic)
  • Base frame

It defines (good to know):

  • Workspace
  • Reach
  • Degrees of Freedom

docs.title: Example: Human Arm
docs.text:
Compare with human arm:

  • Shoulder → Joint 1
  • Elbow → Joint 2
  • Wrist → Joint 3
  • Hand → End-effector

Why this example fits:

The structure is identical: Rigid segments connected by joints producing motion.

docs.title: 3. End-Effector
docs.text:
The end-effector is the part that interacts with the environment.

It is attached at the last link.

Board:

Manipulator → End-effector → Object

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
1) Gripper type Two-finger or mechanical gripping.

2) Anthropomorphic type Human-like robotic hand.

docs.title: Example: Pick-and-Place Robot
docs.text:
In a factory:

  • Arm moves to location.
  • Gripper closes.
  • Object is lifted.
  • Object is placed.

Why this example fits:

The manipulator positions. The end-effector interacts.

Without end-effector: The robot can move but cannot perform tasks.

docs.title: 4. Actuators
docs.text:
Now ask in class:

What makes the joint rotate?

Answer: Actuator.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
An actuator converts energy into motion.

Types:

  • Pneumatic (compressed air)
  • Hydraulic (pressurized fluid)
  • Electric (motor-based)

docs.title: Example Comparison
docs.text:
Industrial heavy press: Hydraulic → high force.

Light packaging robot: Pneumatic → fast, simple.

Precision robot arm: Electric → accurate, easy control.

Why these examples fit:

Different applications require different force, precision, and speed.

docs.title: 5. Transmission System
docs.text:
Important question:

If motor rotates very fast but weak, how do we increase torque?

Answer: Transmission.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
Transmission transfers motion from actuator to joint.

Common types:

  • Belt
  • Chain
  • Gears
  • Link mechanisms

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Motor → Gear → Link

Explain:

Small motor gear drives bigger gear. Torque increases. Speed decreases.

Why this example fits:

Robots often require torque amplification at joints.

docs.title: 6. Complete Motion Flow
docs.text:
Now combine everything:

Sensor says: move Controller computes angle Motor rotates Gear increases torque Link rotates Gripper moves

That is motion subsystem in action.

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text:
Motion system = structure + energy + transmission.

If any part fails:

  • No actuator → no motion
  • No transmission → weak motion
  • No manipulator → no structure
  • No end-effector → no task execution

docs.title: Part 3 — Actuators (Energy to Motion)
docs.text:
We said earlier:

Motion system needs energy.

But what converts energy into movement?

That device is called an actuator.

docs.title: 1. What Is an Actuator?
docs.text:
An actuator is a device that converts energy into mechanical motion.

It produces:

  • Linear motion
  • Rotational motion

Without actuators, the robot cannot move.

docs.title: 2. Types of Actuators
docs.text:
There are three main types used in robotics:

  1. Pneumatic
  2. Hydraulic
  3. Electric

Each uses a different energy source.

docs.title: 3. Pneumatic Actuator
docs.text:
Uses compressed air.

Air pressure pushes a piston. The piston moves linearly.

Characteristics:

  • Fast
  • Simple
  • Clean
  • Light to medium load

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Compressed Air → Cylinder → Piston → Motion (See the image in the slide)

docs.title: Example: Packaging Machine
docs.text:
In packaging systems:

  • Air pushes cylinder
  • Object is pushed quickly
  • Operation repeats rapidly

Why this fits:

Pneumatic systems are:

  • Fast
  • Cheap
  • Suitable for repetitive tasks

But they are not good for:

  • Very high precision
  • Very heavy loads

docs.title: 4. Hydraulic Actuator
docs.text:
Uses pressurized fluid (oil).

Fluid pressure creates very high force.

Characteristics:

  • Very high torque
  • Heavy-duty
  • Powerful
  • Slower than pneumatic

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Pump → Pressurized Oil → Cylinder → Heavy Load Moves (See an animation in the slide)

docs.title: Example: Excavator Arm
docs.text:
Construction machines use hydraulic cylinders.

Why this fits:

Excavator arms:

  • Lift tons of weight
  • Need strong force
  • Operate in harsh conditions

Hydraulics provide: High force with controlled motion.

docs.title: 5. Electric Actuator
docs.text:
Uses electric motors.

Converts electrical energy into rotation.

Characteristics:

  • High precision
  • Easy control
  • Low maintenance
  • Clean operation

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Battery → Motor → Gear → Joint Rotation

docs.title: Example: Industrial Robot Arm
docs.text:
Car manufacturing robot:

  • Uses electric motors
  • Precise angle control
  • Works with digital controller

Why this fits:

Electric actuators:

  • Integrate easily with control systems
  • Provide accurate positioning
  • Require less maintenance

docs.title: 6. When Do We Choose Which?
docs.text:
Ask students:

If I need:

  • Very high force → Hydraulic
  • Very fast simple motion → Pneumatic
  • High precision control → Electric

There is no “best” actuator. There is only “best for the application”.

docs.title: Key Engineering Insight
docs.text:
Actuator choice depends on:

  • Required force
  • Required precision
  • Speed
  • Cost
  • Maintenance
  • Environment

docs.title: Part 4 — Motors
docs.text:
In modern robotics, most systems use electric actuators.

And electric actuators are powered by motors.

So now we ask:

How do different motors work?

There are three common types:

  1. DC Motor
  2. Stepper Motor
  3. Servo Motor

docs.title: Basic Theory
docs.text:
A DC motor converts electrical energy into continuous rotational motion.

Basic parts:

  • Stator (magnetic field)
  • Rotor (armature)
  • Commutator (maintains rotation)

When current flows, magnetic interaction creates torque.

Speed is controlled by: Changing the input voltage.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
Battery → Coil → Magnetic Field → Rotation

Explain:

Current + Magnetic field → Force → Rotation

docs.title: Example: Toy Car
docs.text:
In a toy car:

  • Voltage applied
  • Motor spins continuously
  • Wheels rotate

Why this fits:

DC motor:

  • Simple
  • Continuous rotation
  • No position control by default

docs.title: Limitation
docs.text:
DC motor:

  • Cannot directly control exact angle
  • Needs external feedback for precision

docs.title: Basic Theory
docs.text:
A stepper motor divides a full rotation into equal discrete steps.

Each electrical pulse: → Moves the motor a fixed angle.

Example: 1 pulse = 1.8°

Characteristics:

  • Precise positioning
  • No feedback required (open-loop possible)
  • Holds position when energized

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
Pulse 1 → Step Pulse 2 → Step Pulse 3 → Step

Step by step movement.

docs.title: Example: 3D Printer
docs.text:
3D printer uses stepper motors.

Why this fits:

3D printing requires:

  • Precise position
  • Controlled movement
  • No overshoot

Stepper motors provide controlled discrete motion.

docs.title: Limitation
docs.text:
• Can lose steps under heavy load
  • Less smooth at high speeds

docs.title: Basic Theory
docs.text:
A servo motor is a closed-loop system.

It includes:

  • Motor
  • Feedback sensor
  • Controller

It continuously checks: Desired position vs Actual position.

If error exists: It corrects automatically.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
Desired angle → Compare → Error → Adjust → Correct position

This is feedback control.

docs.title: Example: Robotic Arm Joint
docs.text:
Industrial robot joint:

  • Must reach exact angle
  • Must maintain torque
  • Must react to disturbance

Why this fits:

Servo motor:

  • High precision
  • Real-time correction
  • Stable under load

docs.title: 4. Quick Comparison
docs.text:
DC Motor: Continuous rotation, simple, cheap.

Stepper Motor: Discrete steps, good positioning, open-loop.

Servo Motor: Closed-loop, high precision, industrial use.

docs.title: Engineering Insight
docs.text:
Choose motor based on:

If you need:

  • Simple rotation → DC
  • Precise incremental positioning → Stepper
  • Accurate and stable industrial motion → Servo

There is no universal best motor. Only application-driven selection.

docs.title: Part 5 — Control Hardware
docs.text:
So far we discussed:

  • Motion system
  • Actuators
  • Motors

But now a critical question:

Who controls everything?

Who reads sensors? Who sends motor commands? Who runs algorithms?

That device is the control hardware.

docs.title: 1. What Is Control Hardware?
docs.text:
Control hardware is the physical computing unit that executes robot programs.

It:

  • Reads sensor data
  • Runs control algorithms
  • Sends commands to actuators
  • Maintains timing and coordination

Without control hardware, a robot cannot operate.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
A microcontroller is a compact integrated chip that contains:

  • CPU
  • Memory
  • Input/Output pins
  • Timers
  • ADC (Analog to Digital Converter)

It is designed for:

  • Real-time control
  • Low power
  • Embedded systems

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
Sensor → MCU → Motor Driver → Motor

MCU sits in the middle.

docs.title: Example: Line-Following Robot
docs.text:
A small robot:

  • IR sensor reads line
  • MCU calculates error
  • PWM signal sent to motor

Why this fits:

Microcontrollers:

  • Handle real-time tasks
  • Cheap
  • Low power
  • Ideal for small robots

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Deterministic timing
  • Fast response
  • Limited computing power
  • No operating system (usually)

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
A PLC is an industrial controller designed for:

  • High reliability
  • Harsh environments
  • Deterministic operation
  • Safety compliance

Used mainly in factories.

docs.title: Example: Factory Conveyor System
docs.text:
A PLC:

  • Reads limit switches
  • Controls motors
  • Coordinates robotic arms
  • Runs continuously for years

Why this fits:

Factories need:

  • Reliability
  • Stability
  • Safety
  • Long-term operation

PLC provides industrial robustness.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Extremely reliable
  • Industrial-grade
  • Expensive
  • Not designed for AI

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
An SBC is a small full computer on a single board.

Examples: - Raspberry Pi - Jetson Nano - Tinkerboard

It includes:

  • CPU
  • RAM
  • GPU (sometimes)
  • Operating system

It can run: - Linux - ROS - AI models

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text: Sensor → SBC → AI Model → Decision → Motor Command

docs.title: Example: Autonomous Robot with Vision
docs.text:
A robot using:

  • Camera
  • Object detection
  • SLAM
  • Path planning

Why this fits:

AI and vision require:

  • High computation
  • GPU acceleration
  • Operating system

Microcontrollers cannot handle heavy AI.

docs.title: 5. Quick Comparison
docs.text:
Microcontroller:

  • Real-time
  • Low power
  • Simple control tasks

PLC:

  • Industrial automation
  • High reliability
  • Factory systems

SBC:

  • High computation
  • AI and vision
  • Operating system based

docs.title: Engineering Insight
docs.text:
Often robots use BOTH:

SBC → High-level planning MCU → Low-level motor control

Example:

Camera → SBC → Path plan SBC → MCU → Motor command

This layered architecture is very common in modern robotics.

docs.title: Scenario 1 — Simple Line Follower
docs.text:
A small educational robot:

  • Uses 2 IR sensors
  • Controls 2 DC motors
  • Needs fast response
  • Runs on battery
  • No camera or AI

Question: Which control hardware should be used?

A) PLC B) Microcontroller C) SBC D) Hybrid (MCU + SBC)

Answer: B) Microcontroller

Why:

  • Real-time control needed
  • Low power
  • Simple logic
  • Cheap and compact

Why NOT others:

PLC: - Overkill - Expensive - Designed for industrial systems

SBC: - Too much computation - Higher power consumption

Hybrid: - Unnecessary complexity

docs.title: Scenario 2 — Factory Conveyor System
docs.text:
A factory automation system:

  • Runs 24/7
  • Controls motors and safety switches
  • Must operate reliably for years
  • Safety compliance required

Question: Best device?

A) Microcontroller B) PLC C) SBC D) Arduino

Answer: B) PLC

Why:

  • Industrial reliability
  • Deterministic control
  • Designed for harsh environments
  • Long-term stable operation

Why NOT others:

Microcontroller: - Not industrial-grade - Limited protection

SBC: - Operating system may crash - Not deterministic

Arduino: - Educational tool, not industrial system

docs.title: Scenario 3 — Autonomous Delivery Robot
docs.text:
A campus delivery robot:

  • Uses camera
  • Runs object detection
  • Performs SLAM
  • Path planning
  • Sends data to cloud

Question: Best primary controller?

A) PLC B) Microcontroller C) SBC D) Only DC motor driver

Answer: C) SBC

Why:

  • AI and vision require high computation
  • Needs operating system
  • Supports ROS, deep learning

Why NOT others:

PLC: - Not for AI

Microcontroller: - Cannot handle heavy image processing

Motor driver: - Not a controller

docs.title: Scenario 4 — Smart Robot Architecture
docs.text:
A robot:

  • Uses camera for navigation
  • Uses wheel encoders
  • Needs real-time motor control
  • Runs AI and PID control

Question: Best architecture?

A) Only SBC B) Only Microcontroller C) SBC + Microcontroller D) PLC + SBC

Answer: C) SBC + Microcontroller

Why:

SBC: - High-level planning - Vision - SLAM

Microcontroller: - Low-level real-time motor control

This layered architecture is common in robotics.

Why NOT others:

Only SBC: - OS delays may affect motor control

Only MCU: - Cannot handle AI

PLC + SBC: - Industrial unnecessary complexity

docs.title: Scenario 5 — Heavy Construction Robot
docs.text:
A hydraulic robotic arm:

  • Lifts very heavy loads
  • Operates outdoors
  • Must be highly reliable
  • No AI required

Question: Best control hardware?

A) PLC B) SBC C) Arduino D) Stepper motor

Answer: A) PLC

Why:

  • Industrial-grade
  • High reliability
  • Designed for heavy machinery

Why NOT others:

SBC: - Not rugged enough

Arduino: - Not industrial

Stepper motor: - Not control hardware

docs.title: Scenario 6 — Cost-Constrained Startup Robot
docs.text:
A startup builds a robot:

  • Requires moderate precision
  • No AI
  • Medium load
  • Budget extremely limited
  • Indoor usage only

Question: Best cost-effective solution?

A) PLC B) SBC C) Microcontroller D) Hybrid PLC + SBC

Answer: C) Microcontroller

Why:

  • Budget constraint
  • No AI needed
  • Moderate precision achievable
  • Low cost and power

Why NOT others:

PLC: - Too expensive

SBC: - Unnecessary OS overhead

Hybrid: - Over-engineered

docs.title: Scenario 7 — Safety-Critical Medical Robot
docs.text:
A surgical assistant robot:

  • Requires high precision
  • Must avoid any unpredictable delays
  • Must comply with strict safety regulations
  • Uses image guidance
  • Controls actuators precisely

Question: Best system architecture?

A) Only SBC B) Only PLC C) SBC + Real-time microcontroller D) Arduino only

Answer: C) SBC + Real-time microcontroller

Why:

SBC: - Handles image processing

Microcontroller: - Ensures deterministic control - Real-time safety loop

Why NOT others:

Only SBC: - OS unpredictability risk

Only PLC: - Limited for complex vision AI

Arduino: - Not suitable for medical-grade precision

docs.title: Chapter 2 – Basics of Robotics Kinematics
docs.text:
Kinematics comes from two Greek roots:

  • Kine → motion
  • Matics → related to study or analysis

So, kinematics literally means the study of motion.

In robotics, kinematics answers a very specific and practical question:

How does the motion of joints translate into the motion of the robot’s end-effector?

It deals only with geometry and motion: - positions - orientations - angles - velocities

It does not consider: - forces - torques - masses - energy

That part belongs to dynamics.

In this chapter, we focus purely on kinematics. We learn how joint angles and link lengths determine where a robot’s hand (end-effector) appears in space, and how to compute those angles back from a desired position.

This is the mathematical backbone of: - robot arms - manipulators - pick-and-place systems - surgical robots - industrial automation

In this chapter we study how a robot arm moves in space and how joint angles relate to the position of the end-effector.

We will build everything using pure trigonometry before moving to the DH-parameter method in the next section.

This chapter is divided into three parts:

  1. Forward Kinematics using Trigonometry.
  2. Inverse Kinematics using Trigonometry.
  3. Forward Kinematics using DH Parameters.

docs.title: Part 1 – Forward Kinematics using Trigonometry
docs.text:
We begin with a 3R planar robot: three revolute joints operating in a plane.

The goal of forward kinematics is:

Given joint angles $ \theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3 $, find the position of the end-effector $ P(x, y) $.

docs.title: Basic Idea
docs.text:
For a single rigid link of length \(L\) at an angle \(\theta\) with respect to the x-axis, its endpoint lies at:

\[ x = L \cos \theta, \quad y = L \sin \theta \]

This is simple trigonometry.

However, in a real robot, joint angles are not measured from the global x-axis. Each joint angle is measured with respect to the previous link.

So, to compute the actual \((x, y)\) position of the end-effector, we must reconstruct the absolute orientation of each link using geometry.

docs.title: Two-Link Planar Arm
docs.text:
For a 2-link arm with lengths \(L_1, L_2\) and joint angles \(\theta_1, \theta_2\):

\[ x = L_1 \cos \theta_1 + L_2 \cos \theta_2' \] \[ y = L_1 \sin \theta_1 + L_2 \sin \theta_2' \]

From the geometry of the arm, the effective angle of the second link with respect to the x-axis is:

\[ \theta_2' = -180^\circ + \theta_1 + \theta_2 \]

Substituting:

\[ x = L_1 \cos \theta_1 + L_2 \cos(-180^\circ + \theta_1 + \theta_2) \] \[ y = L_1 \sin \theta_1 + L_2 \sin(-180^\circ + \theta_1 + \theta_2) \]

docs.title: Three-Link Planar Arm (3R)
docs.text:
When the third joint is added, the end-effector position becomes:

\[ x = L_1 \cos \theta_1 + L_2 \cos(-180^\circ + \theta_1 + \theta_2) + L_3 \cos(-360^\circ + \theta_1 + \theta_2 + \theta_3) \] \[ y = L_1 \sin \theta_1 + L_2 \sin(-180^\circ + \theta_1 + \theta_2) + L_3 \sin(-360^\circ + \theta_1 + \theta_2 + \theta_3) \]

These equations give the end-effector position directly from the joint angles.

This method works, but it becomes messy as the number of joints increases. Each new joint introduces more angle bookkeeping and geometric reasoning.

This is exactly why we later move to a systematic and scalable method:

Forward Kinematics using DH Parameters

docs.title: Part 2 – Inverse Kinematics using Trigonometry
docs.text:
Inverse kinematics answers the opposite question of forward kinematics:

Given a target point \(P(x, y, z)\), find the joint angles $ (\theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3) $

For a 3R robot in 3D, we cannot solve this using a single triangle. We must decompose the problem into two geometric views:

  1. Top View → determines \(\theta_1\)
  2. Side View → determines \(\theta_2\) and \(\theta_3\)

This two-view idea is the core trick of trigonometric inverse kinematics.

docs.title: Step 1 – Top View (Finding \(\theta_1\))
docs.text:
Project the point \(P(x, y, z)\) onto the \(XY\) plane.

From the top view:

\[ \tan \theta_1 = \frac{y}{x} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \theta_1 = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \]

We also compute the radial distance:

\[ r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \]

This \(r\) is the horizontal distance from the base to the projection of the end-effector. It becomes the “\(x\)-axis” for the side-view problem.

docs.title: Step 2 – Side View (Finding \(\theta_2\) and \(\theta_3\))
docs.text:
Now work in the \(r\)–\(z\) plane.

Let the base height be \(h\). The effective vertical displacement is:

\[ z' = z - h \]

Form a triangle from the base to point \(P(r, z)\):

\[ AP = \sqrt{r^2 + (z-h)^2} \]

We split \(\theta_2\) into two parts:

\[ \theta_2 = \theta_2' + \theta_2'' \]

The first part comes from simple trigonometry:

\[ \theta_2' = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{z-h}{r}\right) \]

The second part comes from the cosine rule, because this is not a right triangle:

\[ \cos \theta_2'' = \frac{L_2^2 + AP^2 - L_3^2}{2 L_2 \cdot AP} \]

So,

\[ \theta_2 = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{z-h}{r}\right) + \cos^{-1}\!\left( \frac{L_2^2 + AP^2 - L_3^2}{2 L_2 \cdot AP} \right) \]

For the third joint angle:

\[ \theta_3 = \cos^{-1}\!\left( \frac{L_2^2 + L_3^2 - AP^2}{2 L_2 L_3} \right) \]

Finally, from the top view:

\[ \theta_1 = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \]

docs.title: Final Inverse Kinematics Solution
docs.text:
Given a target point \(P(x, y, z)\):

\[ \theta_1 = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \] \[ r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \] \[ AP = \sqrt{r^2 + (z-h)^2} \] \[ \theta_2 = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{z-h}{r}\right) + \cos^{-1}\!\left( \frac{L_2^2 + AP^2 - L_3^2}{2 L_2 \cdot AP} \right) \] \[ \theta_3 = \cos^{-1}\!\left( \frac{L_2^2 + L_3^2 - AP^2}{2 L_2 L_3} \right) \]

These three equations give the complete inverse kinematics solution for the 3R robot.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Inverse kinematics maps position → angles

  • A 3D problem becomes simple when split into:

  • Top view (rotation about base)

  • Side view (planar geometry)

  • We use:

  • Projection
  • Right-triangle trigonometry
  • Cosine rule

This method is intuitive and geometric, but it becomes hard to scale.

That is why, in the next section, we move to a systematic and general method:

In the next part, we will replace this manual geometry with a clean, repeatable framework:

Forward Kinematics using DH Parameters

docs.title: Chapter 2 – Forward Kinematics using Trigonometry
docs.text:
Forward kinematics answers a direct and practical question:

If the joint angles are known, where will the end-effector be?

In other words, forward kinematics maps joint variables to position.

For a robot arm, this means:

  • Input: link lengths and joint angles
  • Output: end-effector position such as \(P(x,y)\)

docs.title: 1. Kinematics in Simple Words
docs.text:
Kinematics is the study of motion without discussing the forces that cause the motion.

In robotics, kinematics tells us how the motion of joints changes the position of the end-effector.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: If a robot arm rotates its joints by certain angles, the hand of the robot moves to a new location. Forward kinematics tells us exactly where that hand goes.

docs.title: 2. Forward Kinematics vs Inverse Kinematics
docs.text:
• Forward Kinematics (FK): joint angles \(\rightarrow\) end-effector position
  • Inverse Kinematics (IK): end-effector position \(\rightarrow\) joint angles

docs.title: Why this example fits
docs.text: In class, when we are given angles and asked to compute \(x\) and \(y\), that is forward kinematics. If instead we are given \(x\) and \(y\) and asked to find the angles, that becomes inverse kinematics.

docs.title: 3. Before Starting FK: Angle Sign Convention
docs.text: Before writing any FK equation, we must define the angle direction correctly.

docs.title: Rule
docs.text:
• Counter-clockwise (CCW) angle = positive
  • Clockwise (CW) angle = negative

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Trigonometric equations depend on angle sign. If we use the wrong sign convention, the final position of the robot will also be wrong.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
If a link rotates \(30^\circ\) counter-clockwise from the positive x-axis, then:

\[ \theta = +30^\circ \]

If it rotates \(30^\circ\) clockwise, then:

\[ \theta = -30^\circ \]

docs.title: Why this example fits
docs.text: Both angles have the same magnitude, but they point in different directions. So the endpoint coordinates will also be different.

docs.title: 4. 3R Planar Robot Setup
docs.text:
We consider a 3R planar robot:

  • \(L_1, L_2, L_3\) = link lengths
  • \(\theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3\) = revolute joint angles
  • Motion is restricted to the XY-plane

docs.title: Important note
docs.text:
• \(\theta_1\) is measured from the global x-axis
  • \(\theta_2\) is measured relative to link 1
  • \(\theta_3\) is measured relative to link 2

This is why FK becomes a little more careful than basic geometry.

docs.title: 5. Start from the Simplest Case: Single Link
docs.text:
Consider one link of length \(L_1\) making angle \(\theta_1\) with the x-axis.

The endpoint is:

\[ x = L_1 \cos \theta_1 \] \[ y = L_1 \sin \theta_1 \]

docs.title: Why this works
docs.text:
This is just basic trigonometry:

  • horizontal part = adjacent side = \(L_1 \cos \theta_1\)
  • vertical part = opposite side = \(L_1 \sin \theta_1\)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
If:

\[ L_1 = 5,\quad \theta_1 = 30^\circ \]

then:

\[ x = 5\cos 30^\circ = 5 \times 0.866 = 4.33 \] \[ y = 5\sin 30^\circ = 5 \times 0.5 = 2.5 \]

So the endpoint is:

\[ P(x,y) = (4.33,\;2.5) \]

docs.title: Why this example fits
docs.text: A single-link robot is the foundation of all multi-link FK. If students understand one link, they can understand multiple links by adding contributions.

docs.title: 6. Two-Link Planar Robot
docs.text:
Now add a second link \(L_2\).

At first glance, we may think:

\[ x = L_1 \cos \theta_1 + L_2 \cos \theta_2 \] \[ y = L_1 \sin \theta_1 + L_2 \sin \theta_2 \]

But this is not fully correct if \(\theta_2\) is measured relative to link 1.

We need the absolute orientation of the second link with respect to the global x-axis.

From the lecture geometry:

\[ \theta_2' = -180^\circ + \theta_1 + \theta_2 \]

So the correct FK becomes:

\[ x = L_1 \cos \theta_1 + L_2 \cos(-180^\circ + \theta_1 + \theta_2) \] \[ y = L_1 \sin \theta_1 + L_2 \sin(-180^\circ + \theta_1 + \theta_2) \]

docs.title: Why this is needed
docs.text: The second joint angle is not measured from the global x-axis. It is measured from the previous link, so we must convert it into a global direction first.

docs.title: Example idea
docs.text: Think of link 1 as changing the “base direction” of link 2. So link 2’s motion is influenced by both \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\).

docs.title: 7. Three-Link Planar Robot
docs.text:
Now add the third revolute joint.

The end-effector position becomes:

\[ x = L_1 \cos \theta_1 + L_2 \cos(-180^\circ + \theta_1 + \theta_2) + L_3 \cos(-360^\circ + \theta_1 + \theta_2 + \theta_3) \] \[ y = L_1 \sin \theta_1 + L_2 \sin(-180^\circ + \theta_1 + \theta_2) + L_3 \sin(-360^\circ + \theta_1 + \theta_2 + \theta_3) \]

docs.title: Meaning of this equation
docs.text:
Each link contributes one part to the final \(x\) and \(y\):

  • link 1 contributes from \(\theta_1\)
  • link 2 contributes after adjusting its angle relative to link 1
  • link 3 contributes after adjusting its angle relative to links 1 and 2

So FK is basically:

final position = sum of all link contributions

docs.title: 8. Cleaner Extension Form
docs.text:
In the slides, a cleaner form is also shown when the effective angle bookkeeping is simplified:

\[ x = L_1 \cos \theta_1 + L_2 \cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2) + L_3 \cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2 + \theta_3) \] \[ y = L_1 \sin \theta_1 + L_2 \sin(\theta_1 - \theta_2) + L_3 \sin(\theta_1 - \theta_2 + \theta_3) \]

docs.title: Why students should notice this
docs.text:
This form is easier to read and easier to use in numerical problems.

It also teaches an important lesson:

FK equations depend on how the angles are defined.

So always check the angle convention before solving.

docs.title: 9. Step-by-Step FK Calculation Strategy
docs.text: When solving a forward kinematics problem, follow these steps:

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
Write down all known values:

  • link lengths
  • joint angles

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text:
Check the angle sign convention

  • CCW positive
  • CW negative

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text:
Identify whether each angle is measured:

  • from the global axis, or
  • from the previous link

docs.title: Step 4
docs.text: Choose the correct FK equation

docs.title: Step 5
docs.text: Substitute values carefully

docs.title: Step 6
docs.text: Compute final \(x\) and \(y\)

docs.title: 10. Why Forward Kinematics is Important
docs.text:
Forward kinematics is the foundation of robot motion analysis.

It is used in: - robot arm positioning - simulation - path planning - motion visualization - control systems

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
If a factory robot must place an object at a certain point, the controller first needs to know:

“If I rotate my joints like this, where will my hand go?”

That is exactly a forward kinematics question.

docs.title: 11. Summary
docs.text:
Forward kinematics means:

Given the joint angles, find the position of the end-effector.

For a planar manipulator:

  • each link adds its own x- and y-contribution
  • joint definitions matter
  • angle signs matter
  • multi-link FK is built from basic trigonometry

Single-link FK is simple. Two-link and three-link FK require careful angle interpretation.

That is why FK using pure trigonometry is educational, but later we move to a more systematic method using DH parameters.

docs.title: Numerical 1
docs.text:
A single-link planar robot has:

  • \(L_1 = 8\)
  • \(\theta_1 = 60^\circ\)

Find the endpoint position \(P(x,y)\).

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Using:

\[ x = L_1 \cos \theta_1,\qquad y = L_1 \sin \theta_1 \]

So,

\[ x = 8\cos 60^\circ = 8 \times 0.5 = 4 \] \[ y = 8\sin 60^\circ = 8 \times 0.866 = 6.928 \]

docs.title: Example: Solving a 3R-3D Spatial Robot from the Given Figure
docs.text:
In this example, we use the robot shown in the figure below.

From the figure, the given values are:

  • \( l_1 = 20 \)
  • \( l_2 = 14 \)
  • \( h = 18 \)
  • \( \theta_1 = 50^\circ \)
  • \( \theta_2 = 60^\circ \)
  • \( \theta_3 = 95^\circ \)

Our goal is to find the end-effector position:

\[ P(x,y,z) \]

docs.title: Step 1: Understand the Robot Motion
docs.text:
This robot has three revolute joints:

  • \( \theta_1 \): base rotation around the vertical axis
  • \( \theta_2 \): first arm angle
  • \( \theta_3 \): second arm angle

The base joint rotates the arm in the horizontal plane, while the upper links determine the horizontal reach and vertical height.

So we solve the problem in two parts:

  1. Find the arm reach in the vertical plane
  2. Use \( \theta_1 \) to project that reach into \(x\) and \(y\)

docs.title: Step 2: Compute the Horizontal Reach \(d_1\)
docs.text:
From the side view, the horizontal reach comes from the horizontal components of the two links.

\[ d_1 = l_1 \cos \theta_2 + l_2 \cos(-180 + \theta_2 + \theta_3) \]

Substitute the values:

\[ d_1 = 20\cos 60^\circ + 14\cos(-180 + 95^\circ + 60^\circ) \] \[ d_1 = 20\cos 60^\circ + 14\cos (-25^\circ) \]

Now,

\[ \cos 60^\circ = 0.5 \] \[ \cos -25^\circ \approx 0.9063 \]

So,

\[ d_1 = 20(0.5) + 14(0.9063) \] \[ d_1 = 10 + 12.688 \] \[ d_1 \approx 22.68 \]

docs.title: Step 3: Compute the Vertical Height \(z\)
docs.text:
The total vertical position is the base height plus the vertical contributions of the two links.

\[ z = h + l_1 \sin \theta_2 + l_2 \sin(-180 + \theta_2 + \theta_3) \]

Substitute the values:

\[ z = 18 + 20\sin 60^\circ + 14\sin (-25^\circ) \]

Now,

\[ \sin 60^\circ \approx 0.866 \] \[ \sin -25^\circ \approx -0.422 \]

So,

\[ z = 18 + 20(0.866) + 14(-0.422) \] \[ z = 18 + 17.32 - 5.908 \] \[ z \approx 29.4 \]

docs.title: Step 4: Compute \(x\) and \(y\) Using Base Rotation
docs.text:
Now use the base angle \( \theta_1 = 50^\circ \).

\[ x = d_1 \cos \theta_1 \] \[ y = d_1 \sin \theta_1 \]

Substitute:

\[ x = 22.68 \cos 50^\circ \] \[ y = 22.68 \sin 50^\circ \]

Now,

\[ \cos 50^\circ \approx 0.643 \] \[ \sin 50^\circ \approx 0.766 \]

So,

\[ x = 22.68(0.643) \approx 14.578 \] \[ y = 22.68(0.766) \approx 17.373 \]

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
Therefore, the end-effector position is:

\[ P(x,y,z) = (14.57,\;17.37,\;29.4) \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This means the robot end-effector is located at:

  • 14.57 units along the x-axis
  • 17.37 units along the y-axis
  • 29.4 units above the base plane

docs.title: End of This Section
docs.text:
In the next part, we will study how to do the opposite problem:

Given the final position, how do we find the joint angles?

That problem is called Inverse Kinematics.

docs.title: Chapter 2 – Inverse Kinematics using Trigonometry
docs.text:
Inverse kinematics answers the opposite question of forward kinematics:

If the end-effector position is given, what joint angles are required to reach that point?

For a 3R spatial robot, the task is:

  • Input: target position \(P(x,y,z)\)
  • Output: joint angles \(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3\)

This robot operates in 3D space, so solving inverse kinematics directly from one 2D triangle is not enough. To make the problem easier, we split it into two parts:

  1. Top View → find base rotation \(\theta_1\)
  2. Side View → find \(\theta_2\) and \(\theta_3\)

This is exactly the geometric idea shown in the lecture slides. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}

docs.title: 1. Why We Split the Problem into Two Views
docs.text:
The robot has: - one base rotation around the vertical axis - two arm links that move in a vertical plane

So it is easier to solve inverse kinematics in two stages:

docs.title: Top View
docs.text: This tells us how much the robot must rotate around the base to face the target.

docs.title: Side View
docs.text: After the base rotation is known, the remaining problem becomes a 2D geometry problem in the vertical plane.

docs.title: Why this approach fits
docs.text: The robot’s first joint controls horizontal direction, while the upper links control reach and height. So separating the motion into these two views makes the math much simpler.

docs.title: 2. Step 1: Top View – Solve for \( \theta_1 \)
docs.text:
From the top view, the point \(P(x,y,z)\) is projected onto the XY plane.

In this view: - \(x\) and \(y\) are known - the horizontal projection of the arm is \(d\) - the base angle is \(\theta_1\)

From the right triangle in the XY plane:

\[ \tan \theta_1 = \frac{y}{x} \]

Therefore,

\[ \theta_1 = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \]

We also need the projection distance \(d\), because it will be used in the side view:

\[ d = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \]

docs.title: Why this works
docs.text: In the top view, the robot is only rotating about the vertical axis. So the geometry becomes a simple 2D triangle in the XY plane.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
If the target is:

\[ P(x,y,z) = (12,16,25) \]

then:

\[ \theta_1 = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{16}{12}\right) \] \[ \theta_1 = \tan^{-1}(1.333) \] \[ \theta_1 \approx 53.13^\circ \]

and

\[ d = \sqrt{12^2 + 16^2} \] \[ d = \sqrt{144+256} = \sqrt{400} = 20 \]

So from the top view:

  • \(\theta_1 \approx 53.13^\circ\)
  • \(d = 20\)

docs.title: Why this example fits
docs.text: The top view only cares about the horizontal placement of the end-effector. So \(x\) and \(y\) are enough to determine the base rotation and projection distance.

docs.title: 3. Step 2: Side View – Convert to a 2D Geometry Problem
docs.text:
Now we move to the side view.

In this view: - horizontal coordinate becomes \(d\) - vertical coordinate is \(z\) - base height is \(h\) - links are \(L_2\) and \(L_3\)

The point becomes:

\[ P(d,z) \]

We define the distance from point \(A\) to the target \(P\) as \(AP\).

From the triangle:

\[ AP^2 = d^2 + (z-h)^2 \]

Since \(d^2=x^2+y^2\), this can also be written as:

\[ AP = \sqrt{x^2+y^2+(z-h)^2} \]

docs.title: Why this works
docs.text: After solving the base angle, the remaining motion happens in one vertical plane. So now the robot becomes a standard 2-link inverse kinematics problem.

docs.title: 4. Solve for \( \theta_2 \)
docs.text:
From the lecture slides, \(\theta_2\) is divided into two parts:

\[ \theta_2 = \theta_2' + \theta_2'' \]

Where:

  • \(\theta_2''\) comes from the right triangle involving \(d\) and \(z-h\)
  • \(\theta_2'\) comes from the cosine rule in triangle \(CAP\)

docs.title: 4.1 First Part: \( \theta_2'' \)
docs.text:
From the right triangle:

\[ \tan \theta_2'' = \frac{z-h}{d} \]

So,

\[ \theta_2'' = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{z-h}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\right) \]

docs.title: 4.2 Second Part: \( \theta_2' \)
docs.text:
Using the cosine rule in triangle \(CAP\):

\[ \cos \theta_2' = \frac{L_2^2 + AP^2 - L_3^2}{2L_2AP} \]

So,

\[ \theta_2' = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{L_2^2 + AP^2 - L_3^2}{2L_2AP}\right) \]

docs.title: 4.3 Final Formula for \( \theta_2 \)
docs.text:
Therefore,

\[ \theta_2 = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{L_2^2 + AP^2 - L_3^2}{2L_2AP}\right) + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{z-h}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\right) \]

docs.title: Why this split is needed
docs.text: One part gives the direction of the line from base shoulder to the target, and the other part gives the internal geometric angle of the arm triangle. Adding them gives the final shoulder angle.

docs.title: 5. Solve for \( \theta_3 \)
docs.text:
From triangle \(CAP\), again using the cosine rule:

\[ \cos \theta_3 = \frac{L_2^2 + L_3^2 - AP^2}{2L_2L_3} \]

So,

\[ \theta_3 = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{L_2^2 + L_3^2 - AP^2}{2L_2L_3}\right) \]

This gives the elbow angle.

docs.title: 6. Final Inverse Kinematics Equations
docs.text:
So the final results are:

\[ \theta_1 = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \] \[ \theta_2 = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{L_2^2 + AP^2 - L_3^2}{2L_2AP}\right) + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{z-h}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\right) \] \[ \theta_3 = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{L_2^2 + L_3^2 - AP^2}{2L_2L_3}\right) \]

where

\[ AP = \sqrt{x^2+y^2+(z-h)^2} \]

These are the same inverse-kinematics formulas developed in the RK2 slides. :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}

docs.title: Step 1: Compute \( \theta_1 \)
docs.text: \[ \theta_1 = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{16}{12}\right) \] \[ \theta_1 \approx 53.13^\circ \]

docs.title: Step 4: Compute \( \theta_2'' \)
docs.text: \[ \theta_2'' = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{25-10}{20}\right) \] \[ \theta_2'' = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{15}{20}\right) \] \[ \theta_2'' \approx 36.87^\circ \]

docs.title: Step 5: Compute \( \theta_2' \)
docs.text: \[ \theta_2' = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{15^2+25^2-12^2}{2\times 15\times 25}\right) \] \[ \theta_2' = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{225+625-144}{750}\right) \] \[ \theta_2' = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{706}{750}\right) \] \[ \theta_2' \approx \cos^{-1}(0.9413) \] \[ \theta_2' \approx 19.73^\circ \]

docs.title: Step 6: Compute \( \theta_2 \)
docs.text: \[ \theta_2 = \theta_2' + \theta_2'' \] \[ \theta_2 = 19.73^\circ + 36.87^\circ \] \[ \theta_2 \approx 56.60^\circ \]

docs.title: Step 7: Compute \( \theta_3 \)
docs.text: \[ \theta_3 = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{15^2+12^2-25^2}{2\times15\times12}\right) \] \[ \theta_3 = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{225+144-625}{360}\right) \] \[ \theta_3 = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{-256}{360}\right) \] \[ \theta_3 \approx \cos^{-1}(-0.7111) \] \[ \theta_3 \approx 135.32^\circ \]

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text:
\[ \theta_1 \approx 53.13^\circ \] \[ \theta_2 \approx 56.60^\circ \] \[ \theta_3 \approx 135.32^\circ \]

So the robot joint angles required to reach \(P(12,16,25)\) are:

\[ (\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3) = (53.13^\circ,\;56.60^\circ,\;135.32^\circ) \]

docs.title: Practice Problem: 3R Spatial Robot Inverse Kinematics
docs.text: The following figure shows a 3R spatial robot manipulator. The end-effector position is known, and the task is to determine the joint angles.

Find the three joint angles:

\[ \theta_1,\;\theta_2,\;\theta_3 \]

docs.title: Final Answer (Check Only)

docs.text:
Inverse kinematics maps:

\[ P(x,y,z)\rightarrow(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3) \]

So, unlike forward kinematics, where we compute position from known angles, inverse kinematics computes the required angles from a known target position.

This is why inverse kinematics is one of the most important tools in robot motion planning and control.

docs.title: 1. Motivation: Why Do We Need a Systematic Method?
docs.text:
In the previous lecture, we solved forward kinematics using trigonometry.

Although this approach works for simple robots, it has several limitations:

  • The method becomes complicated when the robot has many links.
  • It is not systematic, meaning every robot requires a new geometric derivation.
  • If the joint orientation changes, the whole derivation must be redone.
  • It becomes very difficult to extend this method to 3D robot manipulators.

Because of these limitations, robotics researchers introduced a standard mathematical framework called the Denavit–Hartenberg (DH) Parameter Method.

The DH method provides a structured way to describe the geometry of a robot and is widely used in robotics software and industrial robot modeling.

docs.title: 2. What are DH Parameters?
docs.text:
The Denavit–Hartenberg convention is a systematic method to describe the relative transformation between consecutive robot links.

Instead of manually writing equations, each joint is described using four parameters.

These parameters define how one coordinate frame moves relative to the previous frame.

docs.title: DH Parameter Illustration
docs.text:
Add the following image to help visualize the parameters.

Place the image in:

docs.title: 3. The Four DH Parameters
docs.text:
Each joint in a robot is described using four Denavit–Hartenberg (DH) parameters.

Parameter Name Meaning \(a_i\) Link Length Distance between \(z_{i-1}\) and \(z_i\) measured along \(x_i\) \(d_i\) Joint Offset Distance between \(x_{i-1}\) and \(x_i\) measured along \(z_{i-1}\) \(\alpha_i\) Link Twist Angle between \(z_{i-1}\) and \(z_i\) measured about \(x_i\) \(\theta_i\) Joint Angle Angle between \(x_{i-1}\) and \(x_i\) measured about \(z_{i-1}\)

Each of these parameters represents a geometric relationship between two adjacent links.

docs.title: 4.1 Link Length \(a_i\)
docs.text:
The link length represents the distance between two joint axes.

Mathematically,

\[ a_i = \text{distance between } z_{i-1} \text{ and } z_i \text{ measured along } x_i \]

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Imagine moving from axis \(z_{i-1}\) to axis \(z_i\) only along the \(x_i\) direction.

The distance you travel is the link length.

docs.title: Important Observation
docs.text:
Sometimes the two axes are separated, but not along the \(x_i\) direction.

In that case,

\[ a_i = 0 \]

because DH only measures the distance along the \(x_i\) axis.

docs.title: 4.2 Joint Offset \(d_i\)
docs.text:
The joint offset measures how much the coordinate frame shifts along the previous joint axis.

\[ d_i = \text{distance between } x_{i-1} \text{ and } x_i \text{ measured along } z_{i-1} \]

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Imagine walking from \(x_{i-1}\) to \(x_i\) along the direction of \(z_{i-1}\).

The distance traveled represents the joint offset.

In many planar robots,

\[ d_i = 0 \]

because there is no displacement along the vertical direction.

docs.title: 4.3 Link Twist \( \alpha_i \)
docs.text:
Link twist measures the rotation between the two z-axes.

\[ \alpha_i = \text{angle between } z_{i-1} \text{ and } z_i \text{ measured about } x_i \]

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Rotate the next coordinate frame around the \(x_i\) axis.

The angle created between \(z_{i-1}\) and \(z_i\) is the link twist.

Typical values include:

  • \(0^\circ\)
  • \(+90^\circ\)
  • \(-90^\circ\)

depending on the robot configuration.

docs.title: 4.4 Joint Angle \( \theta_i \)
docs.text:
The joint angle describes the rotation of the joint itself.

\[ \theta_i = \text{angle between } x_{i-1} \text{ and } x_i \text{ measured about } z_{i-1} \]

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Rotate the coordinate frame around the joint axis \(z_{i-1}\).

The angle between \(x_{i-1}\) and \(x_i\) is the joint angle.

For revolute joints, this value changes when the motor rotates.

docs.title: 5. Why DH is Useful
docs.text:
The DH convention allows us to describe complex robots using a simple table representation.

Once the DH parameters are known, we can automatically compute:

  • Forward kinematics
  • Transformation matrices
  • End-effector position

This makes DH parameters a standard method in robotics modeling and simulation.

docs.title: 6. Example: 3R Planar Robot
docs.text:
Now we apply the DH method to a 3R planar robot manipulator.

This robot contains:

  • Three revolute joints
  • Link lengths \(L_1, L_2, L_3\)
  • Joint angles \( \theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3 \)
  • End-effector position \(P(x,y)\)

docs.title: 7. Constructing the DH Table
docs.text:
Using the definitions of DH parameters, we construct the following table.

i \( \theta_i \) \( a_i \) \( d_i \) \( \alpha_i \) 1 \(+\theta_1\) \(L_1\) 0 0 2 \(-\theta_2\) \(L_2\) 0 0 3 \(+\theta_3\) \(L_3\) 0 0

docs.title: Why are many parameters zero?
docs.text:
Because this robot is planar:

  • All joint axes are parallel → \( \alpha_i = 0 \)
  • No vertical displacement → \( d_i = 0 \)

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text:
The Denavit–Hartenberg convention provides a systematic way to represent robot geometry using four parameters per joint.

Once these parameters are known, the robot's kinematics can be derived using matrix multiplication, making the analysis scalable to complex robotic systems.

docs.title: Homogeneous Transformation Matrix
docs.text:
In robotics, we often need to describe both position and orientation of one coordinate frame relative to another. To represent these transformations in a compact and systematic way, we use the Homogeneous Transformation Matrix.

A homogeneous transformation matrix combines:

  • Rotation
  • Translation

into a single 4×4 matrix.

docs.title: Why Do We Need Homogeneous Matrices?
docs.text:
If we use normal vectors, we must treat rotation and translation separately.

However, robot motion usually includes both rotation and translation at the same time.

For example:

  • A robotic arm rotates at a joint.
  • The next link also translates to a new position.

Using homogeneous matrices allows us to combine all transformations into one matrix multiplication.

docs.title: Structure of the Homogeneous Transformation Matrix
docs.text:
The general form of a homogeneous transformation matrix is

\[ T = \begin{bmatrix} R & P \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Where

  • \(R\) → 3×3 rotation matrix
  • \(P\) → 3×1 position vector

More explicitly,

\[ T = \begin{bmatrix} r_{11} & r_{12} & r_{13} & p_x \\ r_{21} & r_{22} & r_{23} & p_y \\ r_{31} & r_{32} & r_{33} & p_z \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

docs.title: Interpretation of the Matrix
docs.text:
Part Meaning \(R\) Orientation of the new coordinate frame \(P\) Position of the new coordinate frame Bottom row Keeps the matrix compatible for transformation operations

So the matrix describes both rotation and translation together.

docs.title: Homogeneous Transformation in Robotics
docs.text:
For a robot, we usually want to know:

  • The position of the end-effector
  • The orientation of the tool frame

To compute this, we multiply the transformation matrices of each link.

For example, if a robot has three joints:

\[ T_0^3 = T_0^1 \; T_1^2 \; T_2^3 \]

Where

  • \(T_0^1\) → transformation from frame 0 to frame 1
  • \(T_1^2\) → transformation from frame 1 to frame 2
  • \(T_2^3\) → transformation from frame 2 to frame 3

The final matrix \(T_0^3\) gives the end-effector pose relative to the base frame.

docs.title: Homogeneous Matrix from DH Parameters
docs.text:
Using DH parameters, the transformation matrix between two links becomes

\[ T_i = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_i & -\sin\theta_i\cos\alpha_i & \sin\theta_i\sin\alpha_i & a_i\cos\theta_i \\ \sin\theta_i & \cos\theta_i\cos\alpha_i & -\cos\theta_i\sin\alpha_i & a_i\sin\theta_i \\ 0 & \sin\alpha_i & \cos\alpha_i & d_i \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

This matrix contains all four DH parameters:

  • \(a_i\)
  • \(d_i\)
  • \(\alpha_i\)
  • \(\theta_i\)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Suppose a robot joint has:

\[ a_1 = L_1, \quad d_1 = 0, \quad \alpha_1 = 0 \]

Then the transformation matrix becomes

\[ T_1 = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_1 & -\sin\theta_1 & 0 & L_1\cos\theta_1 \\ \sin\theta_1 & \cos\theta_1 & 0 & L_1\sin\theta_1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

This matrix describes:

  • rotation by \( \theta_1 \)
  • translation by \(L_1\)

docs.title: Why Homogeneous Matrices Are Powerful
docs.text:
Homogeneous matrices allow us to:

  • Represent rotation and translation together
  • Combine multiple transformations using matrix multiplication
  • Compute forward kinematics systematically
  • Model complex robotic systems

This is why homogeneous transformation matrices are a fundamental tool in robotics kinematics.

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
In robotics,

\[ \text{Robot Pose} = \text{Product of Transformation Matrices} \]

Using DH parameters and homogeneous matrices, we can compute the position and orientation of any link or end-effector in a robot manipulator.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: In this lecture, we introduce the fundamentals of control systems: - What is control theory - Open-loop vs closed-loop systems - Feedback and stability - Performance measures - Why controllers are needed - From diagrams to mathematical models

docs.title: 1) What is Control Theory?
docs.text: Control theory studies how to control the behavior of a system to achieve a desired output.

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
A control system always tries to solve this problem:

  • What I want (desired)
  • What I get (actual)
  • Adjust inputs to reduce the difference

docs.title: Example: Motor Speed Control
docs.text:
• Desired speed = 3 rad/s
  • Actual speed = 2.2 rad/s

Problem: The system is not behaving as expected.

Control theory helps us design a system that reduces this error.

docs.title: Why this example works
docs.text:
• Simple and visual
  • Shows mismatch clearly
  • Introduces the need for control immediately

docs.title: 2) What is a Control System?
docs.text:
A control system consists of:

Input → Controller → Process → Output

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
• Input: Desired value
  • Controller: Decision maker
  • Process: Physical system
  • Output: Actual result

docs.title: Example: Self-Balancing Robot
docs.text:
• Input: Stay upright (angle = 0)
  • Controller: PID
  • Process: Robot + motors
  • Output: Actual angle

docs.title: Why this example works
docs.text:
• Strong robotics connection
  • Easy to visualize
  • Maps directly to real systems

docs.title: 3) Open Loop Control
docs.text:
Open-loop systems do not use feedback.

They apply input and never check the output.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
• Apply voltage to motor
  • Assume it reaches desired speed
  • No measurement is taken

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Desired = 3 rad/s Actual = 2.2 rad/s

Error remains uncorrected.

docs.title: Why this example works
docs.text:
• Clearly shows limitation
  • Demonstrates why feedback is needed

docs.title: Real-life Example
docs.text: Fan speed regulator: - You set speed - Load changes → speed changes - System does not correct itself

docs.title: 4) Closed Loop Control (Feedback)
docs.text:
Closed-loop systems use feedback:

Measure → Compare → Correct

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text: The system continuously checks: "Am I doing the right thing?"

docs.title: Example: Thermostat
docs.text:
• Desired temperature = 25°C
  • Current temperature = 22°C
  • Heater turns ON

System keeps adjusting until the desired value is reached.

docs.title: Why this example works
docs.text:
• Very familiar system
  • Clearly shows feedback behavior

docs.title: Robotics Example
docs.text:
Self-balancing robot:

  • Sensor measures angle
  • Controller adjusts motor
  • Robot stays upright

docs.title: 5) Feedback System Components
docs.text:
A feedback system includes:

  • Controller
  • Sensor
  • Actuator
  • Feedback
  • Error signal

docs.title: Example Mapping
docs.text: Component Example Sensor IMU Controller PID Actuator Motor Error Desired - Actual

docs.title: 6) Stability
docs.text: A system is stable if its output remains bounded over time.

docs.title: Example: Balancing a Pencil
docs.text:
• Disturb the pencil
  • It wobbles
  • Returns to position

docs.title: Why this example works
docs.text:
• Easy to visualize
  • Shows recovery behavior clearly

docs.title: 7) System Performance
docs.text:
We evaluate a system using:

  • Transient response
  • Steady-state response

docs.title: 7.1 Transient Response
docs.text: Behavior before the system settles.

docs.title: Example: Light Switch
docs.text:
• Turn ON
  • Light gradually stabilizes

docs.title: Why this example works
docs.text:
• Everyday experience
  • Clearly shows transition phase

docs.title: 7.2 Steady-State Response
docs.text: Behavior after the system stabilizes.

docs.title: Example: Elevator
docs.text:
• Accelerates
  • Moves at constant speed
  • Stops

docs.title: Why this example works
docs.text:
• Real system
  • Clearly shows steady operation

docs.title: Rise Time (Tr)
docs.text:
Time to go from 10% → 90% of final value

  • Indicates speed of response

docs.title: Peak Time (Tp)
docs.text:
Time to reach first maximum peak

  • Shows how quickly system reacts

docs.title: Maximum Overshoot (Mp)
docs.text:
Amount system exceeds final value

  • Indicates oscillation

docs.title: Settling Time (Ts)
docs.text:
Time to stabilize within tolerance

  • Indicates stability speed

docs.title: 9) Steady-State Error
docs.text: ess = desired - actual

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
• Zero error → perfect system
  • Finite error → small difference
  • Infinite error → system fails

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
• Desired = 3
  • Actual = 2.9

Small steady-state error exists.

docs.title: Example 1: Drone Stabilization
docs.text: Situation: - Wind disturbs drone

docs.title: Desired Behavior
docs.text:
• Low rise time → fast reaction
  • Low peak time → quick correction
  • Small overshoot → acceptable

docs.title: Why this example works
docs.text:
• Safety-critical system
  • Requires fast response
  • Real-world robotics scenario

docs.title: Example 2: Chemical Decay
docs.text: Situation: - Substance decays over time

docs.title: Desired Behavior
docs.text:
• Slow response
  • Smooth decay
  • No oscillation

docs.title: Why this example works
docs.text:
• Opposite of drone example
  • Shows not all systems need speed

docs.title: Key Insight
docs.text: Different systems require different behaviors.

docs.title: 11) Why Do We Need a Controller?
docs.text: Problem: Systems do not naturally behave as desired.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Introduce a controller to:

  • Reduce error
  • Improve stability
  • Adjust response

docs.title: Example
docs.text: PID controller: - Adjusts input - Improves system performance

docs.title: 12) Gain
docs.text: Gain = Output / Input

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Gain shows how strongly the system responds.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Input = 2 Output = 10

Gain = 5

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Changing gain affects:

  • Speed
  • Overshoot
  • Stability

docs.title: 13) From Block Diagram to Mathematics
docs.text:
Block diagrams give intuition, but we need math to:

  • Predict behavior
  • Analyze systems
  • Design controllers

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Relationship between input and output.

docs.title: Why useful
docs.text:
• Simplifies analysis
  • Avoids complex differential equations
  • Works in frequency domain

docs.title: Problem (Time Domain)
docs.text:
• Signals are mixed
  • Hard to analyze

docs.title: Example: Sensor Noise
docs.text:
IMU sensor gives: - real motion - vibration noise - disturbances

All mixed together.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Frequency domain separates signals.

docs.title: Why this example works
docs.text:
• Real robotics problem
  • Shows limitation of time domain
  • Motivates frequency analysis

docs.title: Final Summary
docs.text:
A control system:

  • observes the system
  • compares with desired behavior
  • adjusts inputs

docs.title: Key Ideas
docs.text:
• Open loop → no correction
  • Closed loop → uses feedback
  • Performance matters
  • Different systems need different responses
  • Controllers improve behavior
  • Math helps analyze systems

docs.title: Big Picture
docs.text:
Control systems allow us to:

  • make systems stable
  • improve accuracy
  • design intelligent robots

docs.title: Part A — Conceptual MCQ
docs.text: Choose the BEST answer.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text:
A motor is given a fixed voltage and runs without measuring its actual speed. Which type of system is this?

A) Closed-loop B) Feedback system C) Open-loop D) Adaptive system

Answer: C Explanation: No feedback is used, so the system cannot correct errors.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Which of the following BEST describes feedback?

A) Sending input to system B) Measuring output and using it for correction C) Increasing system gain D) Reducing system speed

Answer: B Explanation: Feedback uses output information to adjust the input.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
Why is closed-loop control preferred over open-loop?

A) It is cheaper B) It is simpler C) It corrects errors automatically D) It removes sensors

Answer: C Explanation: Closed-loop systems adjust input based on output, reducing error.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
Which system requires the FASTEST response?

A) Chemical decay B) Temperature control C) Drone stabilization D) Water tank filling

Answer: C Explanation: Drone must react quickly to disturbances to avoid crashing.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text:
Which system requires a SLOW and smooth response?

A) Self-balancing robot B) Drone stabilization C) Chemical decay D) Motor speed control

Answer: C Explanation: Sudden changes are undesirable in chemical systems.

docs.title: Q6
docs.text:
What does gain represent?

A) Energy consumption B) System stability C) Output-to-input ratio D) Sensor accuracy

Answer: C Explanation: Gain = Output / Input.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text:
A system shows large oscillations before settling. What is most likely high?

A) Rise time B) Overshoot C) Steady-state error D) Gain = 0

Answer: B Explanation: Oscillations indicate high overshoot.

docs.title: Q8
docs.text:
Which parameter tells how fast a system initially reacts?

A) Settling time B) Steady-state error C) Rise time D) Gain

Answer: C Explanation: Rise time measures initial speed of response.

docs.title: Q9
docs.text:
A system reaches the desired value but always stays slightly below it. This is:

A) Infinite error B) Zero error C) Finite steady-state error D) Instability

Answer: C Explanation: A constant difference remains.

docs.title: Q10
docs.text:
Why do we move to frequency domain?

A) To increase system speed B) To avoid sensors C) To separate signals and simplify analysis D) To remove equations

Answer: C Explanation: Frequency domain helps separate noise and simplifies analysis.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text:
What is the main limitation of open-loop systems?

Answer: They cannot correct errors because they do not use feedback. If the output differs from desired value, the system cannot adjust itself.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Explain feedback in one sentence.

Answer: Feedback is the process of measuring system output and using it to adjust the input to reduce error.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
Why is feedback important in robotics?

Answer: Because real-world environments change constantly, feedback allows robots to adapt and maintain correct behavior.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
What is stability?

Answer: Stability means the system output remains bounded and eventually settles after disturbances.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text:
Give one real-life example of closed-loop control.

Answer: Thermostat: It measures temperature and adjusts heating/cooling accordingly.

docs.title: Q6
docs.text:
Why is rise time important for drones?

Answer: Because drones must react quickly to disturbances (like wind) to maintain stability.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text:
Why is overshoot undesirable in some systems?

Answer: Because exceeding the desired value can cause damage or unsafe behavior (e.g., chemical systems, temperature control).

docs.title: Q8
docs.text:
What is steady-state error?

Answer: The difference between desired and actual output after the system has settled.

docs.title: Q9
docs.text:
Why do different systems require different responses?

Answer: Because each system has different goals — some require fast response (drone), others require smooth response (chemical process).

docs.title: Q10
docs.text:
Why do we need controllers?

Answer: Because natural system behavior is often not ideal; controllers help adjust input to achieve desired performance.

docs.title: Part C — Thinking Questions (Optional for Class Discussion)
Q1
docs.text:
What could happen if a drone has very high overshoot?

Answer: It may become unstable and crash due to excessive oscillations.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Can a system be fast but unstable? Explain.

Answer: Yes. A system may respond quickly (low rise time) but overshoot excessively and oscillate, making it unstable.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
Why is a purely reactive system not always sufficient?

Answer: Because it lacks long-term planning and may get stuck or fail to reach goals.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
Why is a purely planning-based system not always practical?

Answer: Because real environments change, and heavy planning can be too slow.

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text:
A good control system balances: - speed - stability - accuracy

And uses feedback to adapt to real-world changes.

docs.title: Lecture Two
docs.text: flkdsj

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
In this lecture, we introduce one of the most widely used controllers in control systems:

  • Proportional (P)
  • Integral (I)
  • Derivative (D)

Together, they form the PID controller.

We will discuss: - why PID is needed - what each term does - how PID affects system behavior - a small worked example - Ziegler–Nichols tuning - conceptual quiz and short questions

docs.title: 1) Why Do We Need PID?
docs.text:
From the previous lecture, we already know that a feedback system may still suffer from:

  • slow response
  • overshoot
  • oscillation
  • steady-state error

So, even if a system uses feedback, it may not behave the way we want.

A PID controller helps improve: - speed - accuracy - stability

docs.title: 2) PID Control Law
docs.text:
The standard PID control law in time domain is:

\[ u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\, d\tau + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt} \]

where:

\[ e(t) = r(t) - y(t) \]
  • \(r(t)\) = reference or desired value
  • \(y(t)\) = actual output
  • \(e(t)\) = error
  • \(u(t)\) = control input

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
A PID controller uses three kinds of information:

  • Present error → Proportional term
  • Past error → Integral term
  • Future trend of error → Derivative term

So PID is powerful because it does not only look at what is happening now. It also considers what has been happening and what is likely to happen next.

docs.title: 3) Proportional Control (P)
docs.text:
The proportional controller uses only the current error:

\[ u_P(t) = K_p e(t) \]

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text:
If the error becomes larger, the control action also becomes larger.

If the error is small, the control action is small.

So proportional control is the most direct and intuitive form of control.

docs.title: Example: Self-Balancing Robot
docs.text:
Suppose a balancing robot tilts by some angle.

  • If the tilt is small, apply small motor correction
  • If the tilt is large, apply stronger motor correction

That means the motor command is proportional to the tilt error.

docs.title: Why this example fits
docs.text: This example fits well because: - the relationship between tilt and correction is direct - students can easily visualize it - it connects naturally to robotics

docs.title: Advantage
docs.text:
• simple
  • fast reaction
  • easy to implement

docs.title: Limitation
docs.text:
Proportional control alone often cannot remove steady-state error.

That means the output may come close to the target, but not exactly reach it.

docs.title: 4) Integral Control (I)
docs.text:
The integral controller uses the accumulated error over time:

\[ u_I(t) = K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\, d\tau \]

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text:
If a small error remains for a long time, the integral term keeps growing.

So even if the present error is small, the controller remembers that the system has been wrong for a while.

That is why integral action helps remove steady-state error.

docs.title: Example: Motor Speed Control
docs.text:
Suppose the desired speed is:

\[ r(t) = 10 \text{ rad/s} \]

but the motor settles at:

\[ y(t) = 9.5 \text{ rad/s} \]

Then the error is:

\[ e(t) = 10 - 9.5 = 0.5 \]

If this error stays for a long time, the integral term accumulates it and increases the input until the output gets closer to the desired value.

docs.title: Why this example fits
docs.text: This example fits because: - it shows a small but persistent error - it explains why proportional control alone may be insufficient - it naturally motivates the need for memory of past error

docs.title: Advantage
docs.text: • removes steady-state error

docs.title: Limitation
docs.text: Too much integral action may cause: - oscillation - slower settling - instability

docs.title: 5) Derivative Control (D)
docs.text:
The derivative controller uses the rate of change of error:

\[ u_D(t) = K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt} \]

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text:
Derivative action looks at how quickly the error is changing.

  • If the error is changing rapidly, derivative action reacts strongly
  • If the error is changing slowly, derivative action is small

So derivative control works like a predictor or damping term.

docs.title: Example: Car Braking
docs.text:
Suppose a car is approaching the target speed very quickly.

Even if the current error is still not zero, the derivative term can detect that the error is dropping fast and reduce the control effort.

This helps avoid overshoot.

docs.title: Why this example fits
docs.text: This example fits because: - it gives strong intuition for "predicting the trend" - students understand braking and damping naturally - it shows why derivative can smooth the response

docs.title: Advantage
docs.text:
• reduces overshoot
  • improves damping
  • helps stabilize response

docs.title: Limitation
docs.text:
Derivative action is sensitive to noise.

Because noise can change rapidly, the derivative term may amplify it.

That is why derivative control is rarely used alone.

docs.title: 6) Full PID Controller
docs.text:
Combining all three terms:

\[ u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\, d\tau + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt} \]

Each term plays a different role:

Term Role \(K_p\) reacts to present error \(K_i\) removes persistent error \(K_d\) reduces overshoot and improves damping

docs.title: Example: Drone Attitude Control
docs.text:
A drone is disturbed by wind.

  • P reacts immediately to the tilt error
  • I removes small long-term drift
  • D prevents oscillation and smooths the motion

docs.title: Why this example fits
docs.text:
This is a very good example because: - drones need fast correction - they must remain accurate - too much oscillation is dangerous

So all three PID terms become meaningful together.

docs.title: Increase \(K_p\)
docs.text: Usually: - rise time decreases - response becomes faster - overshoot may increase

docs.title: Increase \(K_i\)
docs.text: Usually: - steady-state error decreases - accuracy improves - overshoot may increase - settling may become slower

docs.title: Increase \(K_d\)
docs.text: Usually: - overshoot decreases - damping improves - settling may improve - sensitivity to noise increases

docs.title: 8) Small PID Math Example
docs.text:
Consider a simple error signal at some instant:

\[ e(t) = 2 \]

Suppose:

\[ \int_0^t e(\tau)\, d\tau = 5 \]

and

\[ \frac{de(t)}{dt} = -0.4 \]

Let the gains be:

\[ K_p = 3, \quad K_i = 0.5, \quad K_d = 1.2 \]

Then the PID output is:

\[ u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\, d\tau + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt} \]

Substitute the values:

\[ u(t) = 3(2) + 0.5(5) + 1.2(-0.4) \] \[ u(t) = 6 + 2.5 - 0.48 \] \[ u(t) = 8.02 \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• The proportional term contributes most because current error is significant
  • The integral term adds extra correction because past error has accumulated
  • The derivative term subtracts a little because the error is already decreasing

This is exactly how PID balances fast response, accuracy, and damping.

docs.title: 9) Simple Control Example with a Plant
docs.text:
Suppose the plant is approximately:

\[ G(s) = \frac{1}{s+1} \]

If we use a proportional controller only:

\[ C(s) = K_p \]

then the open-loop transfer function becomes:

\[ L(s) = C(s)G(s) = \frac{K_p}{s+1} \]

For unity feedback, the closed-loop transfer function is:

\[ T(s) = \frac{L(s)}{1+L(s)} \]

So,

\[ T(s) = \frac{\frac{K_p}{s+1}}{1+\frac{K_p}{s+1}} = \frac{K_p}{s+1+K_p} \]

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text:
If \(K_p\) increases, the system generally responds faster.

But in more complex systems, increasing \(K_p\) too much can cause oscillation or instability.

This is why tuning matters.

docs.title: 10) Ziegler–Nichols Tuning
docs.text: One classical way to tune PID is the Ziegler–Nichols closed-loop method.

docs.title: Idea
docs.text:
1. Set: $$ K_i = 0, \quad K_d = 0 $$

  2. Increase \(K_p\) gradually until the system produces sustained oscillation

  3. Record:

  4. \(K_u\) = ultimate gain
  5. \(P_u\) = oscillation period

Then use formulas to choose \(K_p\), \(K_i\), and \(K_d\).

docs.title: PID Controller
docs.text:
\[ K_p = 0.6 K_u \] \[ T_i = \frac{P_u}{2} \] \[ T_d = \frac{P_u}{8} \]

and then:

\[ K_i = \frac{K_p}{T_i}, \qquad K_d = K_p T_d \]

docs.title: 12) Small Ziegler–Nichols Example
docs.text:
Suppose after testing the system, you find:

\[ K_u = 20, \qquad P_u = 4 \text{ s} \]

For PID tuning:

\[ K_p = 0.6K_u = 0.6(20) = 12 \] \[ T_i = \frac{P_u}{2} = \frac{4}{2} = 2 \] \[ T_d = \frac{P_u}{8} = \frac{4}{8} = 0.5 \]

Now compute:

\[ K_i = \frac{K_p}{T_i} = \frac{12}{2} = 6 \] \[ K_d = K_p T_d = 12(0.5) = 6 \]

So the tuned PID gains become:

\[ K_p = 12, \qquad K_i = 6, \qquad K_d = 6 \]

docs.title: Why this section is useful
docs.text:
Students often hear that PID tuning is important, but they do not know how to begin.

Ziegler–Nichols gives them: - a practical starting method - a repeatable procedure - a connection between experiment and controller design

docs.title: 13) Limitations of Ziegler–Nichols
docs.text:
Ziegler–Nichols is useful, but not perfect.

It may produce: - aggressive tuning - overshoot - noisy behavior in real systems

So in practice, engineers often: - start with Ziegler–Nichols - then fine-tune manually

docs.title: 14) Final Summary
docs.text:
PID combines: - present error - past error - future trend

That is why it works so well.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• P gives fast reaction
  • I removes steady-state error
  • D improves damping and reduces overshoot
  • PID is powerful because it combines all three
  • Ziegler–Nichols provides a practical tuning method

docs.title: Q1
docs.text:
Which PID term reacts to the current error?

A) Integral B) Derivative C) Proportional D) Sensor

Answer: C

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Which PID term helps remove steady-state error?

A) P B) I C) D D) None

Answer: B

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
Which PID term is most sensitive to measurement noise?

A) P B) I C) D D) All equally

Answer: C

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
If a system responds too slowly, which gain is usually increased first?

A) \(K_p\) B) \(K_i\) C) \(K_d\) D) Sensor gain

Answer: A

docs.title: Q5
docs.text:
If a system has too much overshoot, which term is often useful?

A) P B) I C) D D) Input reference

Answer: C

docs.title: Q6
docs.text:
In Ziegler–Nichols tuning, which values are measured experimentally?

A) \(K_p\) and \(K_i\) B) \(K_u\) and \(P_u\) C) \(K_d\) and \(T_d\) D) rise time and settling time

Answer: B

docs.title: Q7
docs.text:
What does the integral term do when a small error stays for a long time?

A) ignores it B) amplifies noise only C) accumulates it D) cancels derivative action

Answer: C

docs.title: Q8
docs.text:
Why is derivative action usually not used alone?

A) It is too slow B) It cannot handle noise well C) It removes all error automatically D) It does not depend on error

Answer: B

docs.title: Q1
docs.text:
What is the main purpose of PID control?

Answer: To improve system response by reducing error using present, past, and future error information.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Why is proportional control alone often insufficient?

Answer: Because it may leave steady-state error.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
What is steady-state error?

Answer: It is the difference between desired output and actual output after the system has settled.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text:
Why can integral action cause oscillation?

Answer: Because it accumulates past error and may apply excessive correction.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text:
What is the main role of derivative action?

Answer: To predict the trend of error and reduce overshoot.

docs.title: Q6
docs.text:
What is \(K_u\) in Ziegler–Nichols tuning?

Answer: It is the ultimate gain, the proportional gain at which sustained oscillation begins.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text:
What is \(P_u\) in Ziegler–Nichols tuning?

Answer: It is the oscillation period measured at the ultimate gain.

docs.title: Q8
docs.text:
Why is PID widely used in robotics?

Answer: Because it gives a practical balance of speed, accuracy, and stability.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text:
Can a system be fast but still inaccurate?

Answer: Yes. A system may respond quickly but still have steady-state error.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text:
Why is tuning necessary even if the PID formula is known?

Answer: Because different systems behave differently, so the gains must be adjusted to match the plant.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text:
Why is Ziegler–Nichols only a starting point?

Answer: Because it often gives aggressive gains, so practical systems usually need further refinement.

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
A good controller is not just mathematically correct. It must also match the behavior that the real system needs.

That is why understanding the meaning of P, I, and D is just as important as knowing the formula.
